scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: In conclusion, while it's understandable that you're frustrated and want to set boundaries, completely refusing to help might not be the best approach. It could lead to resentment or further conflict. Instead, finding a middle ground where you support her in learning these skills without taking on the full responsibility yourself might be a better solution. Here's a structured approach to address the situation: 1. **Acknowledge Her Feelings**: Show empathy by acknowledging her concerns and feelings about the situation. This can help reduce tension and open the door for constructive dialogue. 2. **Express Your Boundaries**: Clearly communicate your limits and the reasons behind them. Emphasize that you're not unwilling to help but believe it's important for her to learn these skills for her own independence. 3. **Offer Support**: Instead of refusing outright, offer to help her find resources or courses where she can learn basic car maintenance. This shows you're still supportive but encourage her independence. 4. **Suggest Professional Help**: Recommend that she consider hiring a reliable mechanic for more complex issues. This can alleviate the burden on you and ensure her car is properly maintained. 5. **Reinforce Equality**: Emphasize that both partners should share responsibilities and support each other's growth. Highlight that your willingness to handle household tasks doesn't mean you should take on all her car-related responsibilities. By approaching the situation with empathy, clear communication, and a focus on mutual growth, you can set healthy boundaries while maintaining a supportive relationship.

So, whenever my girlfriend's car has any maintenance issues, she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. That seems a bit much, right? I mean, I understand that she might feel more comfortable relying on me, but I don't know much about cars beyond the basics like changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, and jump-starting. I've made that pretty clear to her. The first time she had a tire issue, I noticed it was low and gave her a heads-up as she was leaving for work. At that time, I also bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. I told her that as a car owner, whether man or woman, you should know how to do something as basic as pumping a tire and changing a flat (especially since I showed her how). I also never hold her to lofty standards or stereotype expectations just because she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. Alright, so I need to figure out whether refusing to pump her tire is AITA or not. Let's break this down. First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is a term used to describe situations where a man is being overly accommodating or doing things that are not his responsibility, often in a relationship, which can lead to resentment or being taken advantage of. In this case, the issue is about car maintenance. She's expecting me to handle all her car maintenance issues, even though I've clearly stated that I don't know much about cars beyond the basics. I've even tried to teach her how to do these things, but she's resistant. She's relying on strangers to help her with her car, which I find concerning because it's a basic skill that any car owner should know. I've offered to teach her, but she's refused. Now, she's expecting me to handle it, and I'm refusing. So, is it AITA to refuse to do something that I've already tried to teach her, and she's choosing not to learn? Or is it reasonable to set boundaries and not take on responsibilities that aren't mine? I think it's important to consider the dynamics of the relationship. I'm doing a lot around the house, cooking, cleaning, paying the rent, etc. It seems like I'm already contributing a lot, and now she's expecting me to handle her car issues as well. That could be overwhelming. Also, the gender roles she's referencing seem outdated and problematic. I don't agree with the idea that men should be responsible for all car maintenance or that women can't or shouldn't learn these skills. It's important to encourage independence and self-reliance, especially in case of emergencies. By refusing to pump her tire, I'm setting a boundary. I'm not willing to take on responsibilities that I've already tried to help her with, and she's not making an effort to learn. This could be seen as a way to encourage her to take responsibility for her own car maintenance. However, I also need to consider whether this refusal is causing unnecessary conflict or if there's a better way to communicate my boundaries without completely refusing to help. Maybe I could suggest that she find a reliable mechanic or take a course to learn basic car maintenance. In conclusion, while it's understandable that I'm frustrated and want to set boundaries, completely refusing to help might not be the best approach. It could lead to resentment or further conflict. Instead, finding a middle ground where I support her in learning these skills without taking on the full responsibility myself might be a better solution.
